To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Neighborhoods affect children’s early child development via diverse mechanisms, which are dependent on place‐based (where) and individual (who) characteristics.

socioeconomic status was the most common neighborhood determinant examined in the studies we reviewed, that 15 studies examined mediation, and 22 studies examined moderation effects, that neighborhood social‐interactive mechanisms (e.g., social support and social cohesion) were the most common mediators, and that evidence on child‐ or place‐level moderation effects was not conclusive.

(1) neighborhood characteristics are related to early child development; (2), the relationship is stronger for children in disadvantaged families and neighborhoods; (3) the strongest associations are for neighborhood social‐interactive characteristics (e.g., neighborhood social cohesion and social support), and (4) the strongest associations were observed for children in disadvantaged neighborhoods.
